newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Stalemate reached in Helms-Burton trade row.
newsitem.headline: Stalemate reached in Helms-Burton trade row.

text.p: A diplomatic stalemate has been reached over Washington's anti-Cuba policies, with the U.S. unable to convince its allies to go along with its laws which punish businesses for trading with Havana.

This week's high-profile visit to Europe by U.S. envoy Stuart Eizenstat has done little to ease opposition to the Helms-Burton Act, but diplomats say it has at least provided a way in which the matter can be ignored, if not forgotten.

Despite the tub-thumping responses to the laws from Brussels -- as well as Canada and Mexico -- European diplomats concede Helms-Burton has little to do with international trade and more to do with U.S. domestic politics.

The act -- an amalgamation of decades of U.S. anti-Cuba policy -- looked set to drift through the corridors of Congress until March, when Havana shot down in international airspace two aircraft being operated by a Cuban dissident group.

President Bill Clinton -- who had been warned by his Secretary of State Warren Christoper that Washington's allies would not tolerate extra-territorial laws -- had little with which to mollify an outraged public other than to agree the act's passage.

In July, when it was due to become law, Clinton suspended its practical implications for six months with the promise of an extension should allies join U.S. efforts to isolate the government of Fidel Castro.

Eizenstat -- no stranger to Europe, having served as U.S. ambassador to the EU until earlier this year -- this week unveiled what Clinton was seeking to help him justify a further suspension to Congress.
European diplomats agree the U.S. proposals are modest to say the least.
Saying there was no checklist, Eizenstat called on U.S. allies merely to join "a first, genuine, multinational effort" to bring democracy to Cuba.
This effort would include coordinating government, non-government and private sector dealings with Cuba to ensure any assistance aids the people rather than the administration.
The EU will press ahead with finalising counter-measures to the act but, diplomats say, these are likely to be suspended pending moves from Washington.
Where this end-game could fall apart, however, is at the World Trade Organisation where the EU has yet to decide whether to escalate its complaint to a full dispute.

But diplomats say privately that it would probably take the full implementation of the act for the EU to resort to this. Officials are concerned that -- should the WTO find against the U.S. -- Washington would ignore the ruling by invoking a rarely-used national security interests clause.
Washington has hinted as much and Eizenstat has warned of the damage to the multilateral trading system that such a dispute would cause.
The EU is drafting its Helms-Burton legislation with one eye on a potentially more damaging piece of U.S. legislation -- the so-called D'Amato Bill.

Having already been passed, this law threatens U.S. sanctions against foreign companies making new investments in the oil industries of Libya and Iran -- states which Washington accuses of sponsoring international terrorism.

With the EU relying on 20 percent of its oil exports from these countries -- and European companies being substantially involved -- diplomats are bracing for what is likely to prove a messy, lengthy transatlantic trade dispute.
